title: Properties as Geometry
intro: The standard z-transform properties each do something to the plane: add a pole at the origin, stretch the plane, rotate it, turn it inside out through the unit circle, or stack two surfaces.

blocks.text: Each row below is one property: the move in time, what it does to $X(z)$, and what it does to the picture. $\mathcal{R}$ is the ROC of $X(z)$.
Delay: a pole at the origin

Delaying by $k$ samples multiplies by $z^{-k}$: $k$ more poles at the origin (or $k$ fewer zeros there). On the unit circle $|z^{-k}| = 1$, so the magnitude response does not change; only the phase picks up $-k\omega$. The ROC stays the same, except that $z = 0$ may leave it (or $z = \infty$ join it).
Multiplying by an exponential: stretching the plane

Every pole and zero moves from $p$ to $a p$: the plane is scaled by $|a|$ and turned by $\angle a$, and the surface moves with it. Multiplying $u[n]$ (pole at 1) by $0.8^n$ moves the pole to 0.8, which is exactly how $0.8^n u[n]$ gets its pole. With $a = e^{j\omega_0}$, a pure rotation, this is modulation: the whole frequency response turns round the circle by $\omega_0$.

$z \to 1/z$ sends a point at radius $\rho$ and angle $\omega$ to radius $1/\rho$ and angle $-\omega$. Poles inside the unit circle move outside, the outside of a circle becomes the inside of one, and a right-sided signal becomes a left-sided one. The unit circle maps to itself, so the magnitude response is unchanged (for a real signal) and only the phase flips sign. The two-sided exponential $r^{|n|}$ equals its own reversal, and its poles $r$ and $1/r$ are each other's image.

blocks.tex: (x * y)[n] = \sum_k x[k]\, y[n-k] \;\leftrightarrow\; X(z)\, Y(z), \qquad \text{ROC contains } \mathcal{R}_x \cap \mathcal{R}_y

blocks.text: Convolving in time multiplies the transforms, so the poles and zeros of the two pile together into one plot. In decibels the surfaces add: put two filters in a row and the response in dB is the sum of their responses. A pole of one can cancel a zero of the other, which is how the ROC of the product can be larger than the overlap.
Differentiation in z: multiplying by n

Applied to $a^n u[n]$ this gives $n a^n u[n] \leftrightarrow a z^{-1}/(1 - a z^{-1})^2$: the pole doubles up. That is the ramped exponential in the viewer, and the reason repeated poles mean a factor $n$ in time.

Far from the origin every $z^{-n}$ with $n > 0$ vanishes and only $x[0]$ is left. So the height of the surface far out, beyond all the poles and zeros, is $|x[0]|$. For the 8-sample pulse below it is 1; for the damped sine it is 0, since $\sin 0 = 0$.
A finite pulse: zeros round the circle
The pulse $u[n] - u[n-8]$ (eight samples of 1) shows several properties at once. Its transform is a geometric sum:

The numerator vanishes at all eight eighth roots of unity, $e^{j 2\pi k/8}$. The one at $z = 1$ cancels the denominator's pole, leaving seven zeros spaced $45°$ apart round the unit circle, with seven poles at the origin. On the circle the response is 8 at $\omega = 0$ (all eight samples add up) and exactly 0 at $45°$, $90°$, $135°$ and $180°$: the familiar lobes of a moving average. The seven poles at the origin are the delay of a filter that waits for seven past samples.

blocks.title: Shift and scale
blocks.text: Given $0.5^n u[n] \leftrightarrow z/(z - 0.5)$ for $|z| > 0.5$, find the transform of $0.5^{n-3} u[n-3]$ and of $(-1)^n 0.5^n u[n]$.
solution: Delay by 3: $z^{-3} \cdot z/(z - 0.5) = z^{-2}/(z - 0.5)$, with the same ROC $|z| > 0.5$.
Multiplying by $(-1)^n$ is $a = -1$: $X(-z) = -z/(-z - 0.5) = z/(z + 0.5)$, ROC $|z| > 0.5$. The pole moved from $0.5$ to $-0.5$, a half-turn of the plane.

blocks.title: Two filters in a row
blocks.text: A filter with zeros at $\pm j$ is followed by one with a zero at $-1$. Where are the zeros of the combination, and which frequencies does it block?
solution: Convolution multiplies the transforms, so the zeros are $j$, $-j$ and $-1$. They are on the unit circle at $\omega = 90°$ and $180°$ (and $-90°$), so those frequencies are blocked.
blocks.answer: Zeros at $\pm j$ and $-1$: blocks $90°$ and $180°$.
